text:
The University of Edinburgh traces its origins to a 1557 will by Bishop Robert Reid, which led to a royal charter on April 14, 1582, establishing a college of higher education. It officially opened on October 14, 1583, initially covering liberal arts and divinity. The institution gradually assumed the name University of Edinburgh during the 17th century. In 1708, Principal William Carstares restructured the university, abolishing the regenting system and establishing a Dutch-style system of Professors. The university expanded its faculties, founding Law in 1707, Arts in 1708, and Medicine in 1726. In 1762, the formalization of literature began with the appointment of Reverend Hugh Blair as the first Regius Professor of Rhetoric and Belles-Lettres, making Edinburgh the oldest center of literary education in Britain.
The university was a hub during the Scottish Enlightenment, attracting figures like Adam Smith and David Hume. Significant institutional changes included the Universities (Scotland) Act 1858, which granted the university full authority over its own affairs. Early advocacy for women's education culminated in the "Edinburgh Seven" beginning medicine in 1869, leading to women being admitted to graduate in medicine in 1893. Modern facilities include the BioQuarter campus in the Little France area, housing the Anne Rowling Regenerative Neurology Clinic. In terms of governance, the University Court, General Council, and Senatus Academicus are the three major governing bodies, while the Chancellor, Rector, and Principal are key officials.
